How can a basement dwelling neckbeard transform themselves into an Information Broker?

I'll be honest with you, I lucked out. I used to be a pretty dedicated troll--the old school trolling that got people upset and then made them feel stupid, not this swatting garbage. A friend was impressed with how much information I was able to find on people and asked me to find out what I could about a company. He was impressed and hired me on the spot.

It sounds pretty basic but: learn search operators. And go through API documentation for anything that allows you to search and has an API. You would be surprised how many engines' operators are casually buried in API docs. I was using Twitter's lang: operator for nearly two years before it was widely known and long before Twitter Advanced Search turned into this. All because of a block of sample code that used "lang:en" in it.

Some kind of Computer Science degree would have helped me out. A degree in organizational psychology would be useful, too. I've never bothered to get them, though, because my experience renders them mostly moot.

As far as placed to start, I recommend marketing research firms or any company with a strong analytics department (PornHub is one such place, no joke). You can look into companies like Stratfor, but honestly, they're like a bunch of kids trying to play spy and a lot of what they do is in fact illegal. Tech sector has always been the most receptive in my experience.

Is there one tool with which said neckbeard can play, in order to better understand what your field is like?

Any search engine.

Knowing all the ins and outs of your business, have you become more careful with your own information?

Because it relies so heavily on technology, it's a constantly-evolving field. The ins and outs are always changing, so I'd never claim to know everything. As for being careful with my information... sort of.

I used to try and hide my information, but that just made what information did slip out that much more prominent and easy to tie to other information. Then I switched to polluting my information, which basically means filling it up with useless stuff. But, anyone with a rudimentary knowledge of search operators and good abstract reasoning skills can filter out the garbage. Probably the most useful thing I do is keep some advertiser-accessible information out of date. For instance, I never update my LinkedIn page with my "current" workplace until I've left it for another one. It doesn't stop advertisers and people who want access to the company from contacting me, but it does vastly impact the effectiveness of their sales pitches.

If you don't mind being asked, do you often find many of the requests of clients distasteful, almost delineating your own ethics? (Employee pregnancy, for example.)

Often, no. Most of my clients don't know where the line is, so they rely on my judgment and feedback. I've been asked if I could do things by clients who were unsure about the legality, and I've laid it out for them, put my foot down, and proposed shadier people and services for them to contact/hire if they really wanted to go that route. They never have.

My ethics are very flexible, however. For instance, a lot of information I get comes from unsecured or improperly secured servers. Directly accessing that information is on the darker side of grey when it comes to the law, and in some states outright violates business interference laws.

Once I know that information is there and can be accessed, though, it's usually a trivial matter to find a way to make it show up through a search engine. This way I can transform that otherwise "private" information into "publicly available" information since I'm getting the information from the search engine and not directly from the server. The fact that the search engine is pulling from a server that is not meant to be accessible takes the legal responsibility out of my hands. I'm just a user using Google; how was I supposed to know those PDFs containing all of a competitor's financials weren't meant to be returned to me as a search result?

Which sort of areas do IBs find hard to achieve?

I can't speak for others, but for me it's always been the more traditional financial information types for individuals. These have usually required a PI to get access to.

Have there been any important breakthroughs in IBs recently?

Within the last 20 years, the internet and--without meaning to come off as a conspiracy nut--the Patriot Act (it really was the catalyst for the erosion of privacy and information-sharing protections). Within the last 10, social media. Within the last 5, the way Big Data is managed and accessed, including the standardization of APIs and the popularity of easy-to-comprehend coding/scripting languages (Python, Ruby, PHP/MySQL, HTML5), followed by the prominence of Smart Phones in daily life. SJR34 will be the next big breakthrough if it's signed into law. Make no mistake: I don't want it to be.

You might notice a trend. All of these things made it easier to communicate, generate, and share massive amounts of information hassle-free.
